en: The Vajra-Supreme Taste Dhāraṇī Sūtra, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Buddhayaśas of India during the Northern Wei dynasty.
Thus have I heard. At one time, the Bhagavān was staying at the Adorned Assembly on the left side of the Lesser Snowy Mountains.
He dwelt within the Golden Cave,
accompanied by a great assembly of twelve thousand bhikṣus.
At that time, the Bhagavān...
Having finished his almsround,
he sat cross-legged within the Golden Cave and entered the samādhi called "The Manifestation of All Dharmas."
Once he had entered into samādhi,
the assembly of bhikṣus could no longer see the World-Honored One,
and they said to one another:
"Where is the World-Honored One now?
Where is the Sugata now? At that time, the Tathāgata, by means of his majestic spiritual power, [responded].
He caused the forty-two gods of the Śuddhāvāsa heavens to come to where the Buddha was.
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra and Mahābrahmā, the King of the Thirty-three Heavens,
by virtue of the Buddha’s spiritual power, descended to Jambudvīpa.
They arrived at the place where the World-Honored One was.
At that time, the Śuddhāvāsa devas, Śakra Devānām Indra, the Trāyastriṃśa devas, and the Great Brahmā King did not see the World-Honored One.
They all thought to themselves,
"Where is the World-Honored One now?
Having had this thought, they—
He then saw the World-Honored One within the golden cave, having entered the samādhi of cessation.
At that time, the Śuddhāvāsa devas, Śakra Devendra, the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven, the Brahmā kings, and others were present.
They remained silently before the Tathāgata.
At that time, the World-Honored One arose from samādhi and manifested his supernormal powers,
causing all the bodhisattvas throughout this trichiliocosm to appear.
From those who have first resolved their minds toward awakening up to those who are non-retrogressive,
and even those who have received the prediction of being born in their final life—
all of them came to the village of Adorned.
They gathered at the Golden Cave and approached the place where the Tathāgata was;
by the Buddha’s supernatural power, they remained suspended in mid-air at a height of one tala tree above the ground.
At that time, the youth Mañjuśrī, having known the individual thoughts in the minds of all sentient beings,
immediately entered the samādhi called "Gladdening the Minds of All Sentient Beings."
When the youth Mañjuśrī entered samādhi,
those sentient beings attained a state of unprecedented joy.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Maitreya entered the samādhi of the quiescence of all phenomena.
Having entered into samādhi,
the faculties of that great assembly became tranquil.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Ratnaprabha—
Surrounded by six billion two hundred million bodhisattvas,
he proceeded toward the village of Adorned and arrived at the Golden Cave.
Having reached that place, he entered.
He saw himself in the midst of empty space.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara was surrounded by ninety-two thousand bodhisattvas.
He proceeded toward the village of Alaṃbā and reached the Golden Cave;
having arrived there, he was unable to descend to the ground and remained suspended in mid-air.
Together with all the bodhisattvas, they sat upon lotus flowers.
Having sat upon the lotus flowers,
they attained the samādhi that extinguishes all afflictive hindrances and purifies all sentient beings.
At that moment, they were able to extinguish the greed, hatred, delusion, and other afflictions of all sentient beings.
Then, the Bodhisattva Ratnakośa entered the Great Adornment Samādhi.
Having entered this samādhi, [he...]
In the midst of the void, there were spontaneously formed canopies of blue utpala flowers, red padma flowers, yellow kumuda flowers, and white puṇḍarīka flowers;
they possessed their own radiance, independent of the sun and moon.
At that time, the World-Honored One ascended into the air above and remained there spontaneously,
unmoving and with right mindfulness.
At that time, the youth Mañjuśrī,
standing in mid-air with his upper robe arranged over his right shoulder and palms joined toward the Buddha,
addressed the World-Honored One, saying: "World-Honored One..."
For what cause and for what reason is the World-Honored One now remaining in mid-air, unmoving and with right mindfulness?
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the youth Mañjuśrī, saying:
"Mañjuśrī, I wish to expound for the sake of all bodhisattvas within this realm of empty space the Dharma-gate of the Vajra-Supreme-Taste Dhāraṇī.
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Blessed One, we pray only that the Blessed One will expound for the sake of all bodhisattvas the Dharma-gate of the Vajra-Supreme-Taste Dhāraṇī.
The Buddha said:
Mañjuśrī, within the Vajrottama-rasa-dhāraṇī,
there is no bodhi and no dharmas of the Buddhas.
Although these bodhisattvas desire to attain perfect enlightenment,
within the Vajra-Supreme Flavor Dhāraṇī,
there is neither enlightenment nor any conceptualization of one who awakens to enlightenment.
These bodhisattvas fear the world and desire to enter nirvana;
however, within the Vajra-uttama-rasa-dhāraṇī,
there is no distinction between the world and nirvana.
These bodhisattvas seek out wholesome dharmas; however,
within the Vajrottamā-dhāraṇī, there is no discrimination between the wholesome and the unwholesome.
Although these bodhisattvas desire to cross to the other shore,
within the Vajra-Supreme Flavor Dhāraṇī,
there is no conceptual distinction between this shore, the other shore, or one who reaches the other shore.
Although these bodhisattvas desire to purify worlds,
within the Vajrottamā-dhāraṇī there is no conceptual differentiation regarding the purification of worlds.
These bodhisattvas wish to subdue the māras and their enemies;
yet within this Vajra-Supreme-Taste Dhāraṇī, there is no māra,
no enemy of the māras, and no obstructive discrimination.
These bodhisattvas wish to extinguish the māra of the aggregates, the māra of afflictions,
and the māra of death; yet within the Vajrottamā-dhāraṇī,
there are no names or conceptual distinctions of the aggregates, elements, or sense bases.
These bodhisattvas desire to transcend the realm of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas;
yet, within the Vajrottamā-dhāraṇī, there is no conceptual differentiation of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
These bodhisattvas desire to deliver all sentient beings;
yet within the Vajra-uttarāsvāda-dhāraṇī,
there are no sentient beings and no conceptualization of sentient beings.
These bodhisattvas wish to eliminate afflictions such as greed, hatred, and delusion;
however, within the Vajra-uttarāsvāda-dhāraṇī,
there is no conceptual differentiation of afflictions such as greed and hatred.
These bodhisattvas wish to extinguish darkness; however,
within the Vajrottama-rasa-dhāraṇī, there is neither ignorance nor darkness, nor any conceptual differentiation between them.
These bodhisattvas desire to study the supreme wisdom;
however, within the Vajra-Supreme-Taste Dhāraṇī,
there is no differentiation between supreme wisdom and non-supreme wisdom.
These bodhisattvas wish to eliminate afflictions;
however, within the Vajrottama-rasa-dhāraṇī,
there is neither the stain of affliction nor is there purity.
There is neither discipline nor indiscipline, neither this nor that.
There is no loving-kindness, no compassion, no sympathetic joy, and no equanimity.
There is no giving and no stinginess.
There is neither upholding of precepts nor breaking of precepts;
neither patience nor anger;
neither diligence nor indolence.
There is neither concentration nor distraction;
neither wisdom nor delusion;
neither transgression nor non-transgression, and likewise no śrāvakas.
There are no pratyekabuddhas,
nor any Tathāgatas; there is neither dharma nor non-dharma,
whether shallow or deep.
There are no various distinctions between ignorance and wisdom,
nor even any distinction in the wisdom of realization;
there is neither samsara nor nirvana.
...up to and including the factors of enlightenment;
there are no faculties or powers,
and no four foundations of mindfulness.
There are no four right efforts.
There are no four bases of power, Mañjuśrī.
If a bodhisattva wishes to study this Vajrottamā-rasa-dhāraṇī,
that bodhisattva should not abandon the dharmas of ordinary beings;
they should not realize them, should not discard them, should not transcend them, and should not give rise to non-recollection.
Without practicing, without abandoning, and without seeking pleasure, one proceeds without protection.
One should not give rise to defiled signs regarding the dharmas of ordinary beings,
nor should one give rise to the sign of giving.
One is able to be free from the dharmas of the Buddha and no longer perceive any dharmas of ordinary worldlings. Mañjuśrī,
within the Vajrottamā-rasa-dhāraṇī:
Within the dharmas of ordinary beings there are the Buddha-dharmas and the realization of the Buddha-dharmas;
yet, within the Vajra-uttama-rasa-dhāraṇī,
there is neither realization nor non-realization.
This Vajra-Supreme-Taste Dhāraṇī does not even exist within the Buddha-dharma.
This Vajra-Supreme-Taste Dhāraṇī.
He does not abandon ordinary beings nor does he guard against the dharmas of ordinary beings;
he does not move from the worlds of the Buddhas;
he does not give rise to vows, yet he does not relinquish his vows.
Why is this? Mañjuśrī, this Dharma-gate of the Vajra-Supreme-Taste Dhāraṇī—
It inclines toward greed, hatred, and delusion;
it inclines toward women and men;
and it inclines toward the devas.
It accords with all nāgas;
it accords with all yakṣas and rākṣasas;
it accords with all gandharvas.
He accords with all asuras;
he accords with all garuḍas;
he accords with all kiṃnaras.
He accords with the mahoragas;
he is oriented toward all Buddhas;
he is oriented toward all Dharmas.
It accords with all the Sanghas;
it accords with all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas;
it accords with all those in the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals.

Favorable to the water, favorable to the wind, favorable to fire, favorable to the earth, favorable to the eye, favorable to the ear, favorable to the nose, favorable to the tongue, favorable to the body, and favorable to the mind. Mañjuśrī,
within this Vajrottamā-rasa-dhāraṇī, [these qualities are found].
Mañjuśrī, it accords with all phenomena.
As for every portion of the realm of empty space in the eastern direction, [it is likewise].
Mañjuśrī, all the spatial divisions of the southern, western, northern, and upper and lower directions are entirely compliant with and enter into the realm of space.
"These mantra-words of the Vajra-Supreme-Taste accord with all dharmas.
At that time, the youth Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
in what way is greed a dhāraṇī phrase?
The Buddha said:
Mañjuśrī, as for what is called "desire," that desire does not come from the eastern direction to defile sentient beings.
It does not come from the south, west, north, above, or below to defile sentient beings;
it does not arise from within to defile sentient beings;
nor does it come from without to defile sentient beings.

Mañjuśrī, greed, hatred, and delusion all arise from the conceptualization of the internal mind; thus, one perceives defilement and purity. If there were anyone who could eliminate this defilement and purity, [they would not perceive them].
Then there would be no such thing as a dharma that is realized or not realized.
Mañjuśrī, if a dharma is unarisen, [it cannot be realized].
Since beginningless time, it has neither existed internally nor externally. For this reason,
I say that greed is a *dhāraṇī* phrase.
Mañjuśrī, hatred arises from the internal mind’s anger;
yet that anger and hatred do not belong to the past, the present, or the future.
Mañjuśrī, if past phenomena were capable of arising,
they could not bring about the purification of the dhāraṇī phrases.
"Mañjuśrī, the mind of delusion is also not a dhāraṇī phrase.
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Bhagavān, what is a dhāraṇī? What is a dhāraṇī phrase?"
The Buddha said,
"Mañjuśrī, delusion is ignorance."
All phenomena arise from ignorance; they do not arise from the earth element,
nor do they cling to the earth element.
They do not cling to the water element;
they do not cling to the fire element;
they do not cling to the wind element.
They do not cling to the element of space,
nor do they cling to the element of consciousness; yet it is not that they do not cling.
However, these dharmas are neither defiled nor pure.
Mañjuśrī, if there were any dharma that were defiled, then even space would have to be defiled.
Why is this? Because even the realm of empty space does not possess any phenomena that could act as an obstruction. Mañjuśrī!
Regarding what is called "ignorance mingling with all phenomena," it further causes them to transcend [samsara], for they possess no characteristic of extinction;
this is because emptiness acts as an unobstructed condition for them.
Furthermore, it cannot be seen nor grasped;
because it is not material form (*rūpa*), it cannot be beheld.
It is without bondage and without liberation, without defilement and without attachment.
Because they have attained immeasurable supernormal powers,
there is emptiness, nothingness, and no entities whatsoever, Mañjuśrī.
While remaining in the world, he engages in all the worldly affairs of affliction.
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One,"
“Is it that ignorance neither ceases nor does not cease?
The Buddha said,
“Mañjuśrī, it is so.”
Ignorance is itself clarity;
yet the Buddha-Tathāgata speaks of it as ignorance.
Within the ultimate limit (pūrvakoṭi), there is no such thing as ignorance.
For this reason,
it is called the "phrase of ignorance.
Within the intermediate state as well, there is no ignorance.
In the future limit as well, there is no ignorance.
Mañjuśrī, if there were no ignorance among all phenomena, [how could there be arising?]
How can it be said that one sees?
It is without attachment or defilement, yet likewise without forgetfulness.
Nevertheless, all phenomena possess both purity and defilement, and further manifest the characteristics of obstruction.
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
"There is none,
World-Honored One."
"There is not, O Sugata. Thus it is,
Blessed One."
"How is it that ignorance therein is said to cause defilement?
The Buddha said, "Mañjuśrī,..."
For example, when drilling for fire, there is the fire-drill, the wood to be drilled, and the grass;
because the human hand provides the effort and all these conditions are assembled,
smoke first emerges and subsequently fire is produced.
Yet the fire does not reside within the fire-drill, nor within the act of drilling,
nor in the grass held in the hand;
rather, fire arises through the conjunction of these various conditions.
Mañjuśrī, there is no such thing as delusion;
yet all sentient beings [perceive it].
The fires of pride, greed, hatred, and delusion arise from the notion of a self;
yet these fires of greed and the others exist neither within, nor without, nor in between.
However, Mañjuśrī, for what reason is that which you call "delusion" so designated?
It is called "delusion.
Because all dharmas are ultimately liberated,
it is therefore called delusion.
Mañjuśrī, if all dharmas are ultimately liberated,
this is called the Vajra-Supreme-Taste Dhāraṇī phrase.
At that time, the youth Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One,
is there perhaps a dharma-gate?"
Furthermore, this Dharma-gate brings about the accomplishment of Bodhisattvas,
causing them to attain all samādhis that accord with and incline toward [enlightenment].
The Buddha said:
Mañjuśrī, there is a Dharma-gate; because a bodhisattva accomplishes that Dharma-gate, [he attains this].
Thus, one is able to penetrate all matters;
it is like a single character that expresses hundreds or thousands of words,
yet within that character, there is no end to what can be signified.
They teach all phenomena in accordance with those Dharma-gates;
they manifest such and such Dharma-gates.
Although they manifest such immeasurable Dharma-gates, [they do so without attachment].
Yet they cannot exhaust their unimpeded eloquence;
because they have attained the eloquence of inexhaustible joy in preaching,
they are thus able to manifest inexhaustible eloquence.
Within a single phrase of a dharma-gate,
they cause one to enter all phrases of dharma-gates; within all phrases of dharma-gates,
[they likewise cause entry into a single phrase].
"May they be led into the phrase of the single Dharma-gate.
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying,
"World-Honored One..."
"What color is this dharma?
The Buddha said,
"Mañjuśrī," [it is colorless].
"All dharmas are the celestial gate;
this is a dharani phrase. Mañjuśrī said:
“World-Honored One,
how is it that these dhāraṇī phrases are the gates of the devas?
The Buddha said:
Mañjuśrī, all phenomena abide in the samādhi of quiescence;
this is the dhāraṇī phrase of the bodhisattva’s dharma-gate for entering the characteristics of the heavens.
Mañjuśrī, all phenomena are the Dragon Gate;
this is a dhāraṇī phrase.
Mañjuśrī said, "World-Honored One,
why is this dhāraṇī phrase called the 'Dragon Gate'?"
The Buddha said,
"Mañjuśrī, all dharmas are [revealed] by means of the single-gate (ekākṣaramukha)."
Because they are heard through words,
yet one speaks of words while being without words;
this is the dhāraṇī phrase of the bodhisattva’s dharma-gate for entering the characteristics of the dragon.
Mañjuśrī, all dharmas are the gateway of the yakṣas;
this is a dhāraṇī phrase.
Mañjuśrī said, "World-Honored One,
in what way are these dhāraṇī phrases the gateway of the yakṣas?"
The Buddha said,
"Mañjuśrī, all dharmas enter into the mark of a yakṣa."
Because they are ultimately unarisen.
This, Mañjuśrī, is the dhāraṇī phrase of the dharma-gate for entering the signs of the yakṣas.
"All dharmas are the gate of the gandharva.
This is a dharani phrase. Mañjuśrī said:
“World-Honored One,
why is this dharani phrase the gateway of the gandharvas?
The Buddha said:
Mañjuśrī, all phenomena transcend all calculation;
they are immeasurable and boundless, surpassing even space.
This is the dhāraṇī phrase of the dharma-gate for entering the signs of the gandharvas. Mañjuśrī,
all phenomena are the gate of the asuras.
"This is a dhāraṇī phrase. Mañjuśrī said,
"World-Honored One,"
"How is it that these dhāraṇī phrases are the gate of the asuras?
The Buddha said, "Mañjuśrī," [he replied].
All dharmas accord with all gates;
they cannot be reached by means of names,
nor can they be reached by means of form.
It cannot be reached by sound;
it cannot be reached by fragrance;
it cannot be reached by taste.
It cannot be reached by touch;
it cannot be reached by dharmas;
it cannot be reached even by a Buddha.
It is not something that can be reached by what is non-Dharma; it is not something that can be reached by what is non-Saṃgha; it is not something that can be reached by Śrāvakas.
It is not accessible to pratyekabuddhas,
nor is it accessible to ordinary beings, Mañjuśrī.
All phenomena transcend all reaching and non-reaching,
because they do not arise.
This is the dhāraṇī phrase of the Dharma-gate for entering the characteristics of the asuras, [the bodhisattva].
Mañjuśrī, all dharmas are the gate of the garuḍa;
this is a dhāraṇī phrase.
Mañjuśrī said, “World-Honored One,
why are these dhāraṇī phrases the gateway for the garuḍas?”
The Buddha said,
"Mañjuśrī, all dharmas ultimately do not proceed."
Nor is it that they do not act.

They neither go nor come; they are neither born nor extinguished; they do not abide and have no attachment; they are neither bound nor liberated; they have no dwelling place and no departure. Mañjuśrī!
All phenomena do not abide,
for they abide in the equality of the realm of empty space.
This is the dhāraṇī phrase of the gate of the dharma for entering the form of the garuḍa.
Mañjuśrī, all phenomena are the gate of the kiṃnara.
This is a dhāraṇī phrase.
Mañjuśrī said, "World-Honored One,
why is this dharani phrase the gateway of the kinnaras?"
The Buddha said,
"Mañjuśrī, because all dharmas are devoid of an agent, there is neither an agent nor a seeker."
That which is seen without seeking—
this is the dhāraṇī phrase of the dharma-gate for entering the marks of a kiṃnara, Mañjuśrī.
"All dharmas are the gateway of the mahoragas;
this is a dharani phrase. Thus spoke Mañjuśrī.
“World-Honored One,
in what way are these dhāraṇī phrases the gateway of the mahoragas?
The Buddha said:
Mañjuśrī, all dharmas are eternally luminous, being free from the defilements of all dharmas.
All sentient beings cannot be defiled nor can they be purified,
because of the gateway of the pure dhāraṇī. Why is this?
Mañjuśrī, because all phenomena are ultimately quiescent by nature and do not arise,
this is the dhāraṇī phrase of the dharma-gate for entering the characteristics of the mahoragas.
Mañjuśrī, all dharmas are the gateway of women;
this is a dhāraṇī phrase.
Mañjuśrī said, "World-Honored One,
why is this dharani phrase called the 'Gate of Women'?"
The Buddha said,
"Mañjuśrī, all dharmas are entirely false and illusory."
This is the male gate and this is the female gate;
because one has departed from the female gate,
it is called the "non-affair."
This is the dhāraṇī phrase for the bodhisattva’s gateway of entering the marks of women. Mañjuśrī,
all phenomena are the gateway of the man.
"This is a dhāraṇī phrase. Mañjuśrī said,
"World-Honored One,"
"How is it that these dhāraṇī phrases are the gateway for great beings?
The Buddha said, "Mañjuśrī,..."
Mañjuśrī, regarding all phenomena,
if one does not perceive a person (puruṣa) in the past, the present, or the future, [then they are such].
They are detached from the three realms and do not cling to them;
yet in those places there are neither women nor men—
it is merely a conventional designation.
However, that which is designated by conventional names is quiescent in that state,
yet it is described as defiled;
furthermore, that form depends upon the four great elements.
Because they rely upon the four great elements, one does not perceive arising or ceasing;
all dharmas are ultimately and eternally extinguished.
This is the dharani phrase of the gate of the Dharma for entering the characteristics of a Great Man (mahāpuruṣa).
Mañjuśrī, all dharmas are the gateways to hell;
this is a dharani phrase.
Mañjuśrī said, "World-Honored One,
why is this dhāraṇī phrase called the 'gate of hell'?"
The Buddha said,
"Mañjuśrī, by what characteristics is hell defined?"
Mañjuśrī said, "World-Honored One,
all phenomena have the characteristic of being equal to space."
The Buddha said,
"Mañjuśrī, what do you think?"
"From where does that hell arise?
Mañjuśrī replied, "World-Honored One," and so forth.
All phenomena arise from the characteristics of one's own conceptualization;
because of one's own deluded thoughts,
all ordinary beings bind themselves.
Because of being bound, it is hell; although it does not exist [as a substantial entity],
it causes the experiencer to undergo that suffering.
Mañjuśrī said, "World-Honored One,
it is as if there were a person who, within a dream, saw himself fall into hell."
Having fallen into hell,
they see themselves being burned by hundreds of thousands of fires;
they see their bodies seized and cast into cauldrons of boiling water.
That person sees their body undergoing great suffering and affliction;
seeing themselves being scorched and oppressed by a great fire, they give rise to fear and terror,
and utter these words:
"Extremely painful! Extremely painful!
his relatives come and ask him, "What is it that pains you?"
That person replied,
"I am experiencing the extreme suffering and torment of hell;
great fires are burning me."
He then threw my body back into the cauldron of boiling water.
Speaking thus, he spoke with malice toward his kinsmen.
"I am experiencing the sufferings of hell and enduring great agony. Why do these people ask me,
'What suffering do you have?'"
The relatives said to him, "Do not be afraid now; you were merely asleep.
You have not actually gone from here to there."
Nor does it come from there to here.
Upon hearing this, that person then gives rise to the thought within himself:
"I am in a dream; this is false and not real.
It is illusory, like a magical illusion."
Knowing and seeing it thus, body and mind attain peace.
World-Honored One,
it is as if that which does not exist is spoken of as existing.
Yet they say of themselves, "I have fallen into hell.
World-Honored One,
such is the case with all ordinary worldlings.
Through inverted and false conceptions, though there is in reality no bondage, one gives rise to the perception of a woman;
having given rise to this perception of a woman,
one sees oneself engaging in union with her.
They speak thus: "I am a man and she is a woman;
she is my wife and I am her husband."
Because that person gives rise to various afflictions such as greed, hatred, and delusion,
a perception of something to be done arises within their own mind;
for this reason, [the result follows].
There are various unlawful matters such as quarrels and disputes;
having thus given rise to such quarrels and disputes,
those people develop great resentment.
Because of such inverted perceptions,
after his life comes to an end, he falls into hell and undergoes various sufferings for immeasurable eons.
World-Honored One,
it is just as when those relatives come to that person and say:
"World-Honored One, this sleep of yours neither departs nor arrives.
All ordinary beings are likewise so."
It is spoken of through four inverted false views;
yet in reality, within it there is neither man nor woman,
no sentient being, and no life-force, and so forth.
Because all phenomena are unreal and illusory,
one sees that all phenomena are empty by nature, unarisen, and invisible;
they cannot be conceptually differentiated, nor can they be clung to.
All phenomena are like dreams, like illusions, and like the moon reflected in water.
World-Honored One, among all phenomena, there is nothing that can be defiled, nor anything that cannot be defiled.
World-Honored One,
all dharmas are false, because they arise from falsehood.
Therefore, the Tathāgata says that all dharmas are free from "I" and "mine," because they are far removed from all gates to the hells.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised the youth Mañjuśrī, saying:
Excellent, excellent,
Mañjuśrī! All hells should be viewed in this way.
Mañjuśrī, you have made such a distinction based on what you have seen;
if one sees in this way, [it is so].
There is no hell, nor is there a gate to hell;
that person then attains the patience of the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti) at the time this Dharma-gate of hell is being taught.
Ninety-two thousand bodhisattvas all attained the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena;
having attained this patience, they...
At that time, they raised their voices in unison and spoke these words:
"Excellent, excellent!
This is the domain of all the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas."
And within all dharmas that are without self,
one suddenly attains all Buddha-dharmas.
At that time, the youth Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
World-Honored One,
we only pray that the World-Honored One will explain how all bodhisattvas enter the dharma-gate of non-duality.
Because the bodhisattva has attained entry into the dharma-gate of non-duality,
they attain the non-duality of all dharmas and do not cling to them.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the youth Mañjuśrī, saying: "Mañjuśrī,
when a bodhisattva attains this Dharma-door of entering into the equality of all phenomena and accords with it, they have acquired this correct Dharma-door."
Furthermore, within all afflictions, they perceive the Buddha-dharma and attain eloquence,
becoming skilled in preaching the Dharma.
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
what are the characteristics of that dharma-gate?
The Buddha said:
Mañjuśrī, reflect upon this well; I shall speak it for you.
This Dharma-gate is named "Detachment from All Afflictions."
"Therefore, I have taught this gateway of dhāraṇīs. Mañjuśrī said,
"Excellent, World-Honored One!"
"I pray that you will speak for me;
I shall receive it upon the crown of my head.
The Buddha said:
Mañjuśrī, ignorance is bodhi; this is the gateway of dhāraṇī phrases.
Mañjuśrī said, “World-Honored One,
how is it that ignorance is bodhi?”
The Buddha said,
"Mañjuśrī, it is because there is no ignorance that I speak of 'ignorance'."
If there is no ignorance, then there is no birth.
If there is no birth, then there is no defilement. Mañjuśrī.
Awakening is unstained,
because its nature is pure and its essence is pristine. Mañjuśrī.
I speak of ignorance because I perceive this matter;
it is because it is taught as non-dual, Mañjuśrī.
"I do not apprehend ignorance; therefore, I speak of ignorance.
Mañjuśrī, this is the dhāraṇī phrase of the dharma-gate for entering the characteristics of ignorance.
Mañjuśrī, practicing this is bodhi;
this is the gateway of dhāraṇī.
Why is this? Mañjuśrī, because all phenomena are free from all marks of calculation.
Immeasurable and boundless, its limits cannot be seen;
it follows both the wholesome and the unwholesome,
causing beings to enter the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals.
It does not go from this to that,
nor does it come from that to this;
yet it gives rise to "this" and "that."
Mañjuśrī, all dharmas neither pass away nor come;
they go nowhere and arrive nowhere.
Mañjuśrī, these are the dhāraṇī phrases of the dharma-gate for entering the characteristics of the bodhisattva’s practice. Mañjuśrī.
Consciousness is bodhi;
this is the gateway to the dhāraṇīs. Why is that?
Mañjuśrī, the Tathāgata says that consciousness is false,
because that which is produced by the false appears falsely.
Mañjuśrī, if one seeks all dharmas within these entirely false phenomena and says,
"I have realized the Buddha-dharma, attained perfect enlightenment, and delivered all sentient beings," [this is mere delusion].
I am the most supreme victor in the world;
yet such a person, amidst false dharmas, falsely conceives of bodhi and gives rise to arrogance, thereby deceiving and insulting others.
Mañjuśrī, when I sat at the site of enlightenment, there was no dharma to be realized—
neither this as the dharma of the śrāvakas, nor this as the dharma of the pratyekabuddhas, nor this as the dharma of ordinary beings.
Mañjuśrī, this is the dhāraṇī phrase of the dharma-gate for entering the characteristics of consciousness. Mañjuśrī.
Name-and-form is bodhi.
This is the gateway of dhāraṇī. Why is this?
Mañjuśrī, because name-and-form (nāmarūpa) is not a substantial entity,
it is spoken of by means of sound.
Yet there is nothing that is spoken,
because form has no agent; if there is no agent, [there is nothing spoken].
This is precisely without beginning, middle, or end. Mañjuśrī,
the Tathāgata says that this "self" is bodhi.
Furthermore, because it cannot be seen in the ten directions,
Mañjuśrī, this is the dhāraṇī phrase of the dharma-gate for entering the characteristics of name-and-form (nāmarūpa).
Mañjuśrī, the six sense bases are bodhi;
this is the gateway to dhāraṇī.
Why is this? Mañjuśrī, these sense-bases and so forth—
All these are marks of entry;
all are marks of emptiness and marks of tranquility.
It is not that sentient beings, having seen forms with their eyes, [perceive them as such].
Yet one speaks of the "view of self.
It is the same for the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind; they likewise do not form such a thought.
I am able to discern all phenomena;
it is not by means of visual consciousness that one knows the domain of the ear,
nor by means of auditory consciousness that one knows the domain of the eye.
In this way, the mind cognizes the objects of all phenomena;
yet, all phenomena are not the object of the mind,
because they are mutually contradictory.
Mañjuśrī, all phenomena are without cognition and are free from the characteristics of the mind;
because they are mutually dependent, all phenomena are empty.
Mañjuśrī, if all phenomena are ultimately empty, that is the characteristic of bodhi.
This is the dhāraṇī phrase of the dharma-gate for entering the characteristics of the six sense bases.
Mañjuśrī, contact is bodhi.
This is the gateway of dhāraṇīs. Why is this?
Mañjuśrī, [it is because...]
What is called "contact" (sparśa) consists of the characteristics of form, sound, odor, taste, touch, and mental objects (dharma), Mañjuśrī.
If a phenomenon arises by virtue of contact with its conditions,
and if it arises by virtue of conditions,
and if it is established by virtue of conditions—
That which is named is established through conditions; if it is established through conditions, it is illusory.
If it is illusory, it is ultimately non-existent.
If they are ultimately non-existent, then they are neither born nor extinguished.
Mañjuśrī, the fact that all phenomena lack the characteristics of birth and extinction is bodhi.
Mañjuśrī, these are the dhāraṇī phrases of the dharma-gate for entering the characteristics of touch. Mañjuśrī.
Sensation is bodhi.
This is a dhāraṇī gateway. Why is this?
Mañjuśrī, feeling consists of three types of feeling: namely,
painful feeling, pleasant feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
Mañjuśrī, sensation is neither within, nor without, nor in between.
Mañjuśrī, [it is thus].
“If that sensation is neither internal, nor external, nor in between,
how can there be a being therein who experiences feelings of suffering or pleasure? Mañjuśrī said:
World-Honored One,
all ordinary beings are bound by perversion; thus,
within unreal phenomena, they give rise to feelings of pleasure and feelings of suffering.
World-Honored One,
all phenomena are like illusions;
the nature of all sensations is neither arising nor ceasing.
The Buddha said,
"Mañjuśrī, for this reason I say that sensation is bodhi."
Mañjuśrī, these are the dhāraṇī phrases of the dharma-gate for entering the perception of sensation. Mañjuśrī.
Affection is bodhi;
this is the gateway of dhāraṇī. Why is this?
Mañjuśrī, craving is the cause that gives rise to afflictions. Mañjuśrī.
What do you think?
Suppose, for example, there is a person who, though not having actually obtained a son, forms the notion that he has produced a son.
Now, would that son be born from within him, or would he be born from without?
"Does that person exist?
Mañjuśrī replied, "World-Honored One, [he does]."
That person originally had no son;
how could they give rise to the notion of a son?
The Buddha said:
Mañjuśrī, later that man became a great man;
and through their union, he finally fathered a son.
Mañjuśrī, from what does craving arise?
Does it arise from the past, the present, or the future?
"Is it produced internally? Is it produced externally?
Or is it produced through a combination? Mañjuśrī replied:
World-Honored One,
craving is neither within nor without,
nor does it exist anywhere else as a distinct entity.
The Buddha said,
"Mañjuśrī, who has taught this Dharma as something localized or as an object of cognition?"
"Mañjuśrī, furthermore, who created and who made this craving? Mañjuśrī replied:
“World-Honored One,
that which is produced by the separation from craving has no agent. Mañjuśrī said:
World-Honored One,
because all ordinary beings are bound by the four perversions, they immediately give rise to delusion.
The Buddha said,
"Mañjuśrī, what do you think?"
"If a phenomenon exists, does it exist as something conditioned or as something unconditioned?
Mañjuśrī replied, "World-Honored One," [and continued: "..."
"If all these phenomena are ultimately non-existent,
how could those phenomena have defilement or purification? Mañjuśrī replied:
"No, World-Honored One.
The Buddha said, "Mañjuśrī."
If all phenomena exist,
their directional natures and characteristics cannot be perceived;
they do not arise from within, nor do they arise from without.
Neither defiled nor pure, Mañjuśrī— this is bodhi.
Mañjuśrī, this is the dhāraṇī phrase for the dharma-gate of entering the signs of affection. Mañjuśrī.
"Grasping is awakening;
this is the gateway of dhāraṇī. Mañjuśrī said:
World-Honored One,
you have always taught that all dharmas are neither bound nor liberated.
What, then, do these ordinary worldlings grasp at?
The Buddha said,
"Mañjuśrī, all sentient beings are bound by and attached to form, sound, fragrance, taste, touch, and so forth."
And as for grasping at the five desires, Mañjuśrī, what do you think?
"Can form produce sound?
Mañjuśrī replied, "No,
World-Honored One."
The Buddha said,
"Mañjuśrī, what do you think?"
"Is there any single dharma that can cause an obstruction to a dharma, such that it prevents that dharma from abiding? Mañjuśrī replied,
"No, World-Honored One."
The Buddha said,
"Mañjuśrī, all dharmas are ultimately unarisen and without obstruction."
Those phenomena do not arise from one another, nor do they speak to one another,
and yet they possess no activity;
nevertheless, such discourse exists because those phenomena are ultimately deluded.
Mañjuśrī, for this reason, I say that this grasping is the dhāraṇī gateway of the characteristics of bodhi.
Mañjuśrī, these are the dhāraṇī phrases for the bodhisattva’s entry into the dharma-gate of grasping signs. Mañjuśrī.
This is bodhi; this is the gateway of dhāraṇī. Mañjuśrī said:
“World-Honored One,
the Tathāgata originally taught the Dharma for śrāvakas in order to extinguish all forms of existence.
The Buddha said:
Mañjuśrī, there is this existent dharma;
that which I have spoken of is the mark of a strong man.
Therefore, I speak of this Dharma-gate.
Mañjuśrī, if one perceives all phenomena as being without substantiality, having a nature like empty space.
Then one no longer thinks of any of the Buddha-dharmas. Mañjuśrī,
for this reason I say that there are these bodhi-dhāraṇī phrases.
Mañjuśrī, these are the dhāraṇī phrases for the bodhisattva’s entrance into the dharma-gate of phenomena with signs. Mañjuśrī.
Arising is bodhi;
this is the gateway of dhāraṇī. Mañjuśrī said:
“World-Honored One,
the Tathāgata originally taught all dharmas because he regarded them as faults.
The Buddha said:
Mañjuśrī, as for that which is called "arising," a bodhisattva mahāsattva seeks this dharma of arising but cannot find it.
Because it neither arises nor transforms,
Mañjuśrī, for this reason I say that "arising" is a dhāraṇī phrase of bodhi.
Mañjuśrī, these are the dhāraṇī phrases of the dharma-gate for entering the dharma of the characteristics of arising,
spoken for the sake of awakening.
"May all bodhisattvas swiftly attain eloquence, swift eloquence, and unobstructed eloquence.
At that time, the youth Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One..."
"Bhagavān, for bodhisattvas abiding in what stage do you teach this Dharma?
The Buddha said, "Mañjuśrī,"
If bodhisattvas do not seek awakening, do not rejoice in awakening,
do not give rise to the mind of awakening,
and do not realize the Buddha-dharma.
In impure Buddha-fields, without being moved by greed, hatred, or delusion,
if the mind does not desire to transcend the world.
Nor does he give rise to the thought of delivering sentient beings,
subduing Māra, or desiring to preach the Dharma.
Furthermore, Mañjuśrī, regarding those who do not conceive of duality within those dharmas,
I now teach this Dharma-gate solely for the sake of those bodhisattvas who abide on such a stage.
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
if there are bodhisattvas who are able to receive and uphold this Dharma-gate of the Vajra-Supreme-Taste Dhāraṇī,”
"If one reads it, recites it, or explains it extensively for others,
how much merit will such a person obtain?
The Buddha said:
Mañjuśrī, if any bodhisattvas,
regarding this Vajrottamārasa dhāraṇī dharma-gate, receive it,
uphold it, read it, recite it, or explain it to others;
Such a person is like all Buddhas;
for all Buddhas always abide in equanimity,
and thus they are so regarded by all devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, and others.
One should constantly make offerings to it with such worship. Mañjuśrī,
this is the Dharma-gate of the Vajra-Supreme-Taste Dhāraṇī.
It is fully endowed with and accomplishes immeasurable merit. Mañjuśrī,
this is the Dharma-gate of the Vajra-uttarāsvāda Dhāraṇī.
It is inexhaustible.
While this dharma-gate was being taught,
ten thousand bodhisattvas attained this Vajra-Supreme-Taste Dhāraṇī dharma-gate.
Thirty-two thousand bodhisattvas who had first resolved their minds attained the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).
Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, those bodhisattvas,
and the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, humans, and non-humans [were all present].
Having heard what the Buddha had spoken, they all rejoiced greatly, paid their respects, and departed.
*The Vajra-Supreme Flavor Dhāraṇī Sūtra*
